title: Contentment brings unsurpassed happiness (2.40–2.45)
hook: the fruits of the five observances, and the one Patanjali calls happiness with nothing above it

segments.voice: Yesterday: vaira-tyaga. Around someone truly grounded in non-harm, hostility simply drops away.

A seven-year-old's birthday. For weeks there has been one gift on the list, the only thing that matters. Morning comes, the paper tears, and there it is. Pure joy. By lunchtime it's on the floor and the question has started: what can I ask for next? Nobody's a bad kid here. It's just how wanting works, at seven and at seventy. The new car, the promotion, the house with one more room. Patanjali names one happiness that beats every gift on every list.
screen: `ONE GIFT ON THE LIST.` → `BY LUNCH: WHAT NEXT?` → `ONE HAPPINESS ABOVE EVERY GIFT.`

segments.voice: Sutras 2.40 to 2.45 give the fruits of the five observances, quickly. From cleanliness, a certain distance from your own body, then a clear, cheerful, one-pointed mind. From discipline, the body and senses perfected as impurity burns off. From study, meeting your chosen deity. From surrender to Ishvara, the perfection of samadhi itself. In the middle sits the simplest line. Sutra 2.42: from contentment, unsurpassed happiness. Santosha. Anuttama, the word for unsurpassed, means nothing higher, nothing above it. Not the best happiness so far. The top. The classical commentary backs it up with an old verse. Whatever pleasure desire brings in this world, and whatever great pleasure there is in heaven, together they aren't worth a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes when craving ends. A sixteenth. And contentment here isn't settling. It isn't pretending you don't want anything, or that a hard situation is fine. The commentary describes it as not wanting more than what's already at hand. The birthday child doesn't need a better gift. The gift was never the problem; the asking for the next one was. The verse places the highest happiness not at the end of getting, but at the end of wanting. It doesn't arrive. It's what's left.
screen: `THE FRUITS OF THE OBSERVANCES.` · `FROM CONTENTMENT: NOTHING HIGHER.` · `NOT WORTH A SIXTEENTH PART.` · `NOT SETTLING. THE END OF WANTING.` · then, large: `SANTOSHA.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing that's already here and already enough: the breath arriving without being asked, the chair holding you up, a little warmth in your hands. When the mind starts listing what's missing, the email, the plan, the thing you want next, notice the list and come back to what's enough. You don't have to feel blissful; just let enough be enough.
Anuttama, unsurpassed, nothing higher. Sutra 2.42: from contentment, santosha, a happiness with nothing above it.
Your line: santosha. Nothing sits higher than enough, here or in heaven. That's day four sixty-one.

howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras often single out santosha as a daily practice of accepting what is at hand, and some Hindus link it to gratitude in worship, offering food to God before eating and receiving it back as a blessing.

original.note: Sanskrit santoṣa: contentment, satisfaction; the second niyama, whose fruit in 2.42 is unsurpassed happiness.
